item.title: Seattle Seahawks 2026 trade deadline tracker
item.description: Follow ongoing coverage of the 2026 NFL trade deadline, including whether or not the Seahawks make one more move.
item.content:encoded:
We’ve reached NFL and therefore Seattle Seahawks trade deadline week, which often promises to have some interesting deals and rarely actually materializes. Minor or mid-level deals have happened more recently on deadline day itself, so it’s not like we live in a “nothing happens” world. There have admittedly been prominent in-season trades already this year, including the Quenton Nelson and Jeffery Simmons trades just a couple of weeks ago, as well as Joey Porter Jr going to the Dallas Cowboys, and Marvin Harrison Jr heading for the Houston Texans.

For the second year in a row, the trade deadline is during Week 10. The Seattle Seahawks are usually active during the deadline, and this year they’ve pulled off one major trade. Will John Schneider cook up another midseason masterclass like he did for Leonard Williams, Quandre Diggs, Carlos Dunlap, and other names from previous deadline deals? Follow Field Gulls’ trade tracker coverage throughout Monday and Tuesday, and we’ll see what the Seahawks will do as they look to get back on track after a sputtering 5-4 start.

Have the Seattle Seahawks made any trades during the regular season?

Yes. They acquired longtime Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder.

Who could the Seahawks potentially put on the trade block?

No one immediately springs to mind. The likes of Dante Fowler Jr have rarely played this year but likely wouldn’t fetch much on the trade market. Emanuel Wilson being an unofficial healthy scratch is worth monitoring, although similarly he’s not much of a valuable trade piece, and Seattle may not want to risk moving any capable RB given the injury concerns on the depth chart.

Which positions would the Seahawks potentially be most interested in?

Edge rusher and wide receiver might be two positions of need for Seattle. Rashid Shaheed’s injury and generally underwhelming receiving stats could impact what Seattle does at receiver. The edge rushing room is essentially three deep, and with only Derick Hall and Connor O’Toole under contract beyond 2027, there might be some forward thinking required. The New York Jets’ Will MCdonald IV has reportedly requested a trade and could be one to watch.

When does the NFL trade deadline window close?

At 4 pm ET/1 pm PT on Tuesday, Nov. 10.

Notable NFL trade news (Nov. 9)

  • The Atlanta Falcons have traded safety Jessie Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 second-rounder and a 2028 fifth-rounder.
  • The New York Jets have dealt safety Andre Cisco to the Detroit Lions for a 2028 sixth-rounder.
  • The New Orleans Saints have agreed to draft defensive tackle Davon Godchaux to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2028 sixth-rounder, which could become a 2027 sixth-rounder.

item.title: AFC Playoff Picture: Chiefs keep pace with their Week 9 win
item.description: This is where things stand in the AFC after Kansas City’s sixth win of the season.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs’ 35-12 win over the New York Jets on Sunday only helped the team keep pace with the rest of the AFC playoff contenders leading into a big spot for the conference-leading Buffalo Bills on “Monday Night Football” against the Minnesota Vikings.

The Jacksonville Jaguars started the week off with a 33-10 blowout of the Baltimore Ravens on “Thursday Night Football.” Then, the Cincinnati Bengals put on a show in Madrid, Spain, with a 34-17 win over the Atlanta Falcons.

The Denver Broncos also continued riding fourth-quarter dark magic in a 26-21 road win against the Carolina Panthers, maintaining the lead in the AFC West going into a Week 10 bye.

The biggest result that went Kansas City’s way was the New England Patriots’ 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers. That, and the Cleveland Browns’ overtime loss to the New Orleans Saints. A clear divide now exists between the Top 6 teams in the conference (all with two or fewer losses) and the rest.

AFC playoff standings after Sunday of Week 9

1. Buffalo Bills (6-1) – Monday Night Football

2. Denver Broncos (7-2)

3. Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2, 5-2)

4. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2, win over CIN, 3-2 AFC)

5. Kansas City Chiefs (6-2, 6-1 AFC)

6. Cincinnati Bengals (6-2, loss to PIT, 4-2 AFC)

7. New England Patriots (5-4, 5-1 AFC)

8. Cleveland Browns (5-4, 3-3 AFC)

9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-5, 3-3 AFC)

10. Baltimore Ravens (4-5, 2-4 AFC)

11. Houston Texans (3-5)

12. New York Jets (2-7, 2-4 AFC)

13. Indianapolis Colts (2-7, 1-5 AFC)

14. Miami Dolphins (1-7, 1-4 AFC)

15. Tennessee Titans (1-7, 1-5 AFC)

16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-8)

Explaining the 6-2 logjam in the AFC playoff standings

The Steelers and Bengals are both 6-2, so they first have to settle the AFC North leader. Pittsburgh’s win over the Bengals slots the Steelers into fourth place. 

In the Wild card, the Chiefs and Bengals are tied. The Chiefs have the best AFC record at 6-1, so they fill in at fifth. The Bengals are sixth.

item.title: The Broncos are riding high into their bye after comeback victory over Panthers
item.description: At 7-2, the Denver Broncos are in a great spot entering their bye week. But are they poised to make a splash prior to the trade deadline to bolster their Super Bowl chances?
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos, the comeback kings of the National Football League, pulled off another nailbiter on Sunday. Another impressive fourth quarter comeback was the big factor in their 26-21 win against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday. The Broncos have set a new NFL record with sixteen-straight wins in one-score games. On top of that, they have moved to 7-2 on the season and still hold the top spot in the AFC West.

Another game, another mark in the win column. This year’s Broncos haven’t been at their best. Nevertheless, they’ve reeled off five victories in a row and enter the bye week with a lot of momentum in their favor. Now, Denver gets to enjoy their bye week and will have some much-needed time off to recuperate and recalibrate before their Week 11 matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders.

After yesterday’s victory, Head Coach Sean Payton reflected on the team’s odds-defying streak of wins. The probability of the Broncos winning sixteen of those close affairs in a row? Presumably 150 million to one. While the wins are great, Payton isn’t content and knows the team still has a lot of work to do to get better in the second half of the season.

“Well, part of it pisses me off because there’s been a few of them that you would say shouldn’t have been one-score games and then obviously there’s some that are. Look, they’ve been great. We knew coming in Thursday, we just knew the type of team we were playing,” stated Paton.

“They’ve been doing some really explosive things on offense. They were banged up certainly on defense as we were. We’ll take this break, but we still have to be—and it’s not that you’re never satisfied—but we still have some work to do.”

The Broncos struggled to find an answer to the Panthers’ offensive prowess late in the first half and at the beginning of the second half. Fourth-year quarterback Bryce Young was able to carve up Denver’s depleted secondary and march down the field numerous times to keep them in the game.

At times, the Broncos were their own worst enemies. The penalties and miscues that happened late could have very well cost them the game. But when the stakes were at their highest, the defense was able to force several turnovers and the offense ignited in the fourth quarter to lead the team to their seventh win of the season.

One issue that has plagued Denver all season long was third down conversions. Entering the game, they were one of the league’s worst converting less than 30-percent of those opportunities. Against the Panthers, the team was 6-of-10 and had a hot streak late in the game that was a huge difference maker.

Quite impressive, considering they were down one of their top receiving targets for the entire second half. Quarterback Bo Nix took time after the game to highlight the other wide receivers who stepped up and were clutch when it mattered most.

 “We got plays for Jaylen that somebody else has to step in and take. That’s what, in my opinion, was the fun part of today. That was really cool to see Troy, Pat, and Marvin step up and make plays when their numbers were called,” stated Nix.

“Even though they didn’t have reps at it all week, they studied and knew what they were supposed to do. To me, that’s fun football, when you’re in there and your back’s against the wall and you just have to figure out a way to go get a first down,” added Nix.

Over the first nine weeks of the season, the Broncos have shown a lot of grit and guts. Their resilience is certainly one of their best qualities. No matter how tough things get, they don’t seem to flinch in the face of adversity. In fact, it almost seems like they relish it.

Denver’s second half slate of opponents is much easier than the gauntlet they have faced to start the season. That may give them an inside track to have a shot at the AFC’s top playoff seed for a second consecutive season. However, they will need to play much better overall in order to make that happen.

One question that looms large is whether or not the Broncos’ brass feels confident that the current group of players are good enough to accomplish that. Coach Payton noted he likes this year’s squad, but will certainly be leaving no stone unturned when it comes to potentially making additions before tomorrow’s trade deadline.

“That’s impossible to predict. We’ll discuss what’s out there, and I think we’ll see what happens. But I like this team. There’s room for us to get better, but I like this team a lot. We just got to take advantage of the position we’re sitting in right now.”

At 7-2 and atop the AFC West, Denver is in a great spot. Will they make a big move that can help solidify their status as a true Super Bowl contender? We will know that answer to that in the next thirty hours.

item.title: The Bears needed an ugly win like this. Now, never do it again.
item.description: The Bears found a way to win a game in the most unlikely fashion, but let’s not do that again. @kdthompson5 with more here:
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, it’s good to win ugly. After all, what do you learn from steamrolling everyone and making things look easy all the time?

That’s the silver lining I’m trying to take from the Chicago Bears’ messy 27-24 walk-off win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football. 

I, like many, scoffed at the idea that the then-3-5 Bucs would “humble” the Bears the way several analysts had suggested Tampa would. And for the first quarter or so of action, it looked like we’d be right. 

Unfortunately, we weren’t.

It was terrible football from there on out. Five turnovers (four interceptions, varying in their degrees of bad, and an unfortunate fumble by Luther Burden III while he was concussed). The Bucs willed their way back into the game and eventually tied it up.

The 2025 Bears played and won some rough games, but nothing quite that bad. 

But a win is a win, especially on a short week, and sometimes complementary football requires you to pick up your guys when they’re struggling. The offense did it in Week 1 as the defense couldn’t stop a nosebleed, scoring 59 points. This time, it was the defense’s turn to work their magic. We even got a Jaylon Johnson pick-six, for crying out loud! And in the end, the offense did just enough—thanks to some busted coverages by the Bucs—to seal the deal with Cairo Santos’ 38-yard field goal.

The most important thing: the Bears will go into their bye week at a strong 7-2, with their opportunity to seize the division lead still intact when they return. Get healthy. Learn from the failures of this game. Get back on the horse in Week 11 against the New Orleans Saints.

Also…let’s not do this again.

In the same way as the Bears didn’t need to continually prove their mettle in the clutch the way they did last year, they certainly don’t need to demonstrate they can give the ball away five times and still win every week. That’s not going to cut it.

Get that out of your system, and get back to being locked in and executing at a high level. The 3-5 Saints might not look like much, but they fight.

People are already suggesting the Bucs gave the league the blueprint for how to deal with Chicago’s offense, that this won’t be the last time we see Williams and Ben Johnson struggle like this.

For their sake, the Bears need to make sure it is. Because there’s a reason the 2006 Bears are the only other team in NFL history to win a game that brutal: it simply isn’t a winning formula.

The good news is that, as easy as it would’ve been for them to lose, they made the choice not to mail it in. And that counts for something. Specifically, it’s another positive number in the win column.

item.title: Kevin Stefanski on Jessie Bates trade: Falcons aren't punting on the season
item.description: The Falcons traded veteran safety Jessie Bates to the Jaguars today, which some might see as a sign that the Falcons don't see themselves as contenders and are looking ahead at 2027.
item.content:encoded:
The Falcons traded veteran safety Jessie Bates to the Jaguars today, which some might see as a sign that the Falcons don't see themselves as contenders and are looking ahead at 2027. Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski says that's not the case.

Stefanski did acknowledge that the Falcons are building for the future, but he also noted that in the NFC South, Atlanta remains very much in contention at 3-6.

"You guys know how I feel about Jessie the person, Jessie the player," Stefanski told reporters. "But at the same time, this is football, where sometimes you have one foot in the short term, one foot in the long term. There's things like this that make your team better in the long run. Draft picks are the life blood of an organization. That's something we believe in.

Stefanski said he wants fans to know that they still are going to compete to win the NFC South.

"Our fans are smart enough to know that in no way, shape or form would we punt on this season. We have three wins, just like the rest of our division. Obviously not where we want to be, we want to play better, but we're in the thick of this thing and we trust in the guys we have," Stefanski said.

The Falcons might not be punting on the season, but they are deciding to move on from a player who can help them this season and get draft picks for future seasons. The Falcons still might win the worst division in football, but today's trade is not the trade pf a team that thinks it's a Super Bowl contender this year.

item.title: Ben Brown injury forces Patriots to once again adjust their O-line
item.description: The veteran offensive lineman won’t make the trip to Germany, per head coach Mike Vrabel.
item.content:encoded:
While wide receiver A.J. Brown might be making the trip to Germany this week alongside the rest of the New England Patriots, another member of the team’s starting lineup will not be available for the upcoming game against the Detroit Lions.

Guard Ben Brown, who exited Sunday’s loss to the Green Bay Packers with a knee injury, will be out this week. Head coach Mike Vrabel confirmed his status during a press conference on Monday.

“He won’t make it this week,” Vrabel told reporters from the Gillette Stadium podium.

Starting the Packers game at left guard, Brown remained down after suffering a knee injury late in the second quarter. He departed for the blue medial tent on the sideline and later the locker room, and was initially announced as questionable to return. However, he never made his back onto the field.

In Brown’s place, Walter Rouse finished the game at left guard. Based on the personnel available, Rouse is also likely to draw the start against the Lions.

That said, Vrabel did not rule out the possibility of his team activating fellow interior lineman Greg Van Roten from injured reserve in the coming days.

“That’s something that we’ll look at,” Vrabel said. “He’s eligible and has been working hard to get back. So, we’ll take a look at that and see where he is tomorrow or Wednesday when we practice.”

The Patriots entered the 2026 regular season with Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu as their starting guard. However, Onwenu was lost to an achilles fracture in Week 2, followed by his backup Van Roten going down with a thigh injury just one week later. Brown was the next man up at that point, but he himself was hurt in Week 6 against the New York Jets — the same game that saw Vera-Tucker go down as well.

Unless Van Roten is indeed activated and reinserted into the lineup, the Patriots are looking at Rouse and Matt Pryor starting at left and right guard, respectively, against the Lions in Week 10.

item.title: Where will this Eagles season rank among the all-time worst?
item.description: The 2026 season has been an unexpected, and unwelcome, addition to the worst Eagles teams of the last 40 years.
item.content:encoded:
There was a time when virtually every Eagles season was like this.

Prior to 1988, the autumn was generally a depressing time in Philadelphia. There were very few seasons to celebrate. But since Buddy Ryan broke through with the first of his three straight playoff appearances in ‘88, the Eagles have been one of the marquee teams in the NFL. Their .575 winning percentage over the last 39 seasons is 5th-best, with only the Chiefs (.578), Patriots (.596), Packers (.602) and Steelers (.611) better.

Seasons like what we’re experiencing now have been few and far between over that stretch. After another brutal offensive showing with their fourth quarterback in a 19-11 loss to the Giants at Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday, Nick Sirianni’s Birds have lost seven in a row and dropped to 2-7 on the season. This would be just the 10th losing season in the last 39 for the Eagles. They are in last place in a laughingly bad NFC East, having lost to each of their three divisional opponents in three consecutive weeks by a combined score of 84-42.

And while it’s highly unlikely the team will lose their final eight games and finish 2-15 this year, it’s difficult right now to envision how they’re ever going to win again.

When all is said and done, will this be the worst Eagles team of the last 40 years? There are four other squads they’ll have to contend with for that dubious honor. Let’s take a look at how this year’s Eagles, through nine games, compare with the very worst of the last four decades.

View Link

There are a few key terms that are helpful to know more about.

Yards +/- quantifies the difference in yards gained and yards allowed and where that team ranks in the NFL. The higher the number, the worse the ranking. Strength of Schedule helps paint a picture of how difficult a schedule the Eagles had to deal with that year. Negative numbers mean an easier schedule. Margin of Victory is the average difference in score per game. SRS is a metric by Pro Football Reference called Simple Rating System that takes into account margin of victory and strength of schedule and provides a number relative to average (0.0), that can be considered a point spread. So, a -6.7 SRS means that team, on average, would have been a 6.7 point underdog. OSRS and DSRS measure offensive and defensive Simple Rating System.

Based on the numbers, the 1998 season is quite clearly the worst team the franchise has fielded in the last 40 years, and it actually isn’t all that close. Ray Rhodes’ final campaign was an utter disaster. Their -183 point differential and -11.4 point margin of victory drove their -12.8 SRS that was far and away the lowest of any of the five teams we’re discussing.

As painful as the 2026 offense has been to watch, Rhodes’ ‘98 team averaged 10.1 points per game against one of the easiest schedules in the NFL that season. Koy Detmer, Bobby Hoying and Rodney Peete “led” an offense that scored 20+ points just ONCE , in a Week 4 24-21 loss to the Chiefs. They didn’t score more than 17 points in any of their final 12 games, and they were shut out three times that season. Somehow Duce Staley ran for 1,065 yards, and Jeff Graham was their top receiver in yards (600). They threw 7 touchdowns as a team and tossed 18 INTs.

Defensively, they had nine interceptions as a defense, with Brian Dawkins, Troy Vincent and Mike Zordich with two each. Hugh Douglas piled up 12.5 sacks, and the legendary Al Wallace was 2nd, with 6. It was a tough watch.

Incredibly, the team made a highlights video for this unit, entitled “A New Beginning.” You’ll notice most titles of highlight videos of terrible teams that resulted in the firing of a head coach have similar themes.

“A New Beginning.” “A New Era Begins.” “Into The Great Wide Open.” “Free Fallin’.” Sorry, those last two were just Tom Petty songs.

And they got 23 whole minutes out of it, although much of the play was in slow motion, which helped take up some time.

The 2012 season was just slightly worse from an SRS perspective (-8.9) compared to this year’s team (-8.8). Their -10.3 point margin of victory was 2nd-worst, with an offense that was slightly more functional than this year’s group, but a worse defense.

This was Andy Reid’s final season and, coming off an 8-8 record the year before, got off to a 3-1 start thanks to several last-second victories. The team then completely fell apart, losing 10 of their last 11 in what was clearly the end of an era. Mike Vick, who led the team on a miraculous run in 2010, couldn’t duplicate that feat and made just 10 starts for the 2012 Birds. Nick Foles, the back-up, made the other six. Outside of the QB, however, there were building blocks on that offense, including LeSean McCoy, DeSean Jackson, Jeremy Maclin, Jason Avant and Brent Celek.

The defense started the season with Juan Castillo, the team’s long-time offensive coordinator, leading the defense for a second season, but he was replaced by Todd Bowles midway through the year. The defense gave up 30+ points in 7 of their last 10 games, and at least 25 in 27 or more in 9 of their last 10. This was one of the few cases where the defense was the weaker link.

The team’s season highlight video was titled “A Season of Change.” That’s putting a positive spin on things.

With half a season in the books, the 2026 Eagles’ SRS would put them 3rd on this list of awful teams, but nipping at the ‘12 Eagles’ heels. Just below them is the pandemic Birds of 2020.

The entire country was desperate for live sports during the height of COVID, but fans in Philadelphia quickly reconsidered that desire watching this team play. But with fake, cardboard cutout fans in the stands “watching,” the Eagles in Doug Pederson’s final season in Philadelphia played like fake, cardboard cutouts themselves.

At least the players didn’t have to deal with fans booing inside the stadium. And for 2020, the team didn’t even bother with a full highlights package. Instead, they put together a compilation of the best plays only from their victories. Pretty smart, if you ask me.

The Eagles were three seasons removed from their first Super Bowl title but even fresher off a wild card loss to the Seahawks at home in which Carson Wentz, playing in his first playoff game, was concussed in the first half. He never recovered from his litany of injuries and led an absolutely dreadful offensive effort in which he threw an NFL-leading 15 interceptions with a QB rating of 72.8. He was also sacked a league-high 50 times, with rookie Jalen Hurts eventually taking over for the final four games of the season.

Those Eagles had a point differential of -84. By comparison, this year’s Birds have a point differential of -73. So this year’s team is on pace to blow past that number. That team averaged 20.9 points per game, this year’s Eagles are averaging 16.4. And at least that squad had an interesting young quarterback to get excited about.

Last, the 1999 Eagles. This season launched the Andy Reid era, one of the most successful and exciting runs in franchise history. But it was a slow build under then-QB Doug Pederson, who tried to guide a brand new offensive system while rookie first round pick Donovan McNabb got his feet wet. Once McNabb got comfortable, the team played pretty well over the final three weeks, and it was clear this was an improving roster with competent coaching.

And yet, the ‘99 Eagles finished 30th in the NFL in terms of yardage differential. This year’s Eagles are 31st, 2nd-worst in the league. But I’d say, right now, the ‘26 Eagles are worse than Reid’s first year in Philadelphia.

Honorable mention must be given to the 1994 Eagles, who started 7-2 in Rich Kotite’s final year with the team, only to lose their last seven to finish 7-9, as well as the 2015 7-9 season, Chip Kelly’s final year. The records and overall numbers don’t put them in this same stratosphere, but they were truly terrible, too.

In all but one of these seasons, the head coach was fired at the end of it. Nick Sirianni, despite two Super Bowl appearances, five straight playoff seasons and one championship, is likely to join Rhodes, Andy and Doug in suffering the same fate.

Of course, there are still eight more games left in this lost season. So much can happen, both good and bad. But right now, here are my rankings, from worst-to-“first”:

  • 1998: Ray Rhodes’ Disaster
  • 2012: Andy’s Goodbye
  • 2026: Nick’s Last Gasp?
  • 2020: COVID & Doug
  • 1999: Andy’s First Season

Do you agree? Will this season surpass 2012 and 1998?

item.title: Jaguars double down on defense, trade for Davon Godchaux
item.description: The Jaguars are ALL IN on 2026, adding further reinforcements to their defense
item.content:encoded:
The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t messing around.

Just hours after agreeing a blockbuster trade for Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates III, the Jaguars have returned to the negotiating table, acquiring New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux in a second significant defensive addition ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline.

According to reports, Jacksonville will send a 2028 sixth-round pick to New Orleans in exchange for the veteran defensive tackle. The selection could be upgraded to a 2027 sixth-round pick if the Jaguars acquire one through the compensatory selection process, or via another trade.

It’s another relatively modest price for an experienced NFL starter, but the bigger picture is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: Jacksonville are going all-in.

What does Davon Godchaux bring to Jacksonville?

At 6-foot-3 and 330 pounds, Godchaux brings some considerable bulk to the Jaguars’ defensive interior.

The 31-year-old was originally selected by the Miami Dolphins in the fifth round of the 2017 NFL Draft, spending four seasons in South Florida before moving to New England in 2021. He subsequently spent four seasons with the Patriots before returning to his home state of Louisiana with the Saints in 2025.

Godchaux has built a reputation as a run-stuffing defensive tackle, providing a sizeable presence in the middle of the defensive line. He isn’t somebody Jacksonville should expect to transform their pass rush, however.

Across 144 career appearances, including 128 starts, he has recorded 486 tackles and 5.5 sacks. His value comes primarily from his ability to occupy blockers, hold his ground against the run and make life more difficult for opposing offenses between the tackles.

There is an obvious need for that in Jacksonville. The Jaguars have lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton to a season-ending quadriceps injury, leaving a gaping hole in the middle of their defensive front. Godchaux provides an experienced replacement who can contribute immediately, rather than asking the coaching staff to rely exclusively on younger, less experienced options.

His 2026 production hasn’t been particularly impressive, with 14 tackles in seven appearances for New Orleans and no sacks. There are legitimate questions about how much he has left to offer at this stage of his career.

Nevertheless, Jacksonville isn’t acquiring Godchaux to be a superstar. They’re acquiring him to provide some much-needed depth and physicality at a position where they have been hit by injury.

A familiar face for Anthony Campanile

There is another interesting aspect to this acquisition: Godchaux has previous experience working within a coaching staff led by Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile.

Campanile spent four seasons as the Miami Dolphins’ linebackers coach between 2020 and 2023. Godchaux was also in Miami from 2017 through 2020, meaning the pair overlapped during the 2020 season.

That familiarity could prove useful as Godchaux makes the transition to Jacksonville. Campanile knows the type of player he is getting, while Godchaux should have some understanding of the defensive philosophy and coaching expectations that Jacksonville are trying to establish.

It’s worth remembering that Campanile was coaching the linebackers rather than the defensive line in Miami, and their shared time was relatively brief. Godchaux was placed on injured reserve in October 2020 after appearing in five games. Still, there is a connection there, and the familiarity certainly won’t hurt when it comes to integrating a midseason acquisition.

Campanile has already demonstrated his ability to build a formidable defensive unit in Jacksonville. Godchaux gives him another experienced body to work with as the Jaguars attempt to maintain that standard through the second half of the season.

Jaguars trade grade: B

This is a sensible piece of business from Jacksonville.

A sixth-round selection for a veteran defensive tackle with 128 career starts is a relatively small investment, particularly when the team has an immediate need at the position.

Godchaux isn’t going to solve every problem on the defensive line, and his declining production this season means there is some risk attached to the acquisition. There’s also the faint sting of reality after star names like Jalen Carter and Christian Barmore were bandied around as potential options. 

However, Jacksonville isn’t paying a premium for a player who needs to develop. They’re bringing in somebody who has spent almost a decade in the NFL and understands the demands of playing defensive tackle at the highest level. The injury to Hamilton makes this move particularly understandable.

It’s not a spectacular acquisition, but it addresses a genuine weakness without costing the Jaguars significant draft capital.

The Jaguars are ALL IN

Perhaps the most significant part of this trade isn’t actually the player Jacksonville has acquired. It’s what the move represents. The Jaguars had already made a substantial statement with the Jessie Bates trade; a genuine difference-maker at safety who brings elite experience, ball skills and leadership to the back end of Campanile’s defense.

Now, they’ve followed that up by addressing another defensive weakness with the acquisition of Godchaux. That’s two defensive reinforcements in a single day, with the Jaguars surrendering considerable future draft capital to improve their chances of competing right now.

Jacksonville entered the deadline at 6-2, leading the AFC South and looking increasingly like a legitimate contender in the AFC.

There is little point pretending these moves come without risk. Bates is in the final year of his contract, and Godchaux is a veteran whose best football may already be behind him. The Jaguars are also reducing their collection of future draft picks, limiting some of the flexibility they would otherwise have had.

But this is what competing for a Super Bowl looks like. The Jaguars have a talented roster, an explosive offense under Liam Coen and a defense that has already demonstrated its ability to compete with the best in the league. They have identified weaknesses, recognised an opportunity and acted decisively to address them.

The Bates acquisition was the headline move. Godchaux is the reinforcement that helps make the first deal even more meaningful. Jacksonville isn’t sitting back and hoping their current roster is good enough – they’re making sure of it. And with time still left on the trade deadline clock, don’t be surprised if the Jaguars aren’t finished just yet.

item.title: The NFL’s Other Credibility Problem: Replays
item.description: Hiding your officiating is not helpful
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a rough year for NFL officiating, as penalties are way up in frequency and, as a result, calls are still having a major impact on games. This has beendiscussed to death; however, I wanted to raise the additional issue of the NFL’s broadcast partners’ complicity.

Yesterday, late in the Packers-Patriots game, when the Packers had victory well in hand, and backup quarterback Tommy DeVito had replaced Drake Maye, the officials made a call that, in the grand scheme of things, didn’t matter. Patriots right tackle Caleb Lomu completely blew a block on Packers edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton, who capitalized by forcing a rushed throw from DeVito. Dennis-Sutton made some light contact with DeVito just after the throw, best described as “maybe a light push” or perhaps “brushing by.” Here, take a look.

Dennis-Sutton was flagged for a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty on this play for the love tap, which is ridiculous, but if you were watching the game, you probably didn’t know how ridiculous it actually was. You see, Fox never showed a replay, which would have almost certainly led to yet another discussion of how the league is protecting quarterbacks to an absurd extent, or worse.

Let’s talk about the “or worse” because while this play did not have an impact on the outcome of the game, it absolutely did have an enormous impact on the outcome of the drive. The result of this play would have been a third and goal from the Green Bay eight-yard line, and a good chance that they Packer defense holds the Patriots to either three or zero points, depending on how aggressive they wanted to be. Instead, the call gifted the Pats a first down at the Packer four-yard line, and on second down, backup running back Corey Kiner punched it in from the four, cutting the Packer lead to 45-27. The Pats would fail on the two-point try after a false start penalty.

Major League Baseball has suffered several pitch-rigging scandals in the last year, where bettors conspired with pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz to throw specific pitches for balls in order to win hundreds of thousands of dollars. With live-action betting now ubiquitous, it is now possible to bet on individual events that don’t matter (much) to the overall outcome of a game, and with it comes extra temptation.

One of the best ways to defend against such things (other than reversing course on the ubiquity of gambling) is to cover your games as transparently as possible, so that at the very least, anything suspicious is out in the open. The NFL, along with its broadcast partners, too often opts for the alternative, where they elect not to show replays of controversial or poor calls if they can avoid it. Sometimes this is impossible, but every football fan has experienced a play where they are screaming at their TV about not getting a replay.

That strategy may have worked in 1996, but here in 2026 all it did was send me and several of my colleagues looking for the clip the following day because we were all wondering what we missed. It turned out what we missed was an extremely bad call that gifted the Patriots an extra three-ish (or six-ish) points. I have no issues assuming that a random poor call is just a mistake; however, once people start trying to hide things from me, they lose the benefit of the doubt. The league has an officiating problem this year. If they’re not going to show it and talk about it, I’m going to assume they are in on it. I am quite sure I am not alone.

item.title: New York Jets trade defensive back for 2028 draft pick
item.description: The Jets make their first move as the NFL trade deadline approaches
item.content:encoded:
The Andre Cisco era is over for the New York Jets. Actually, that’s a misnomer. These days we seem to always designate something an era that in no way merits the term. Andre Cisco falls firmly in that category.

The New York Jets have traded backup safety Andre Cisco to the Detroit Lions for a 2028 sixth round draft pick. That’s better.

The Jets originally acquired Andre Cisco by signing him as an unrestricted free agent in 2025. Cisco was brought in expecting to be a playmaker in the back end of the defense, but it did not work out that way. After eight weeks of uninspired play in 2025 in which Cisco racked up zero interceptions, one pass defended, one tackle for loss and one fumble recovery, with little in the way of defensive playmaking, Cisco’s 2025 campaign ended with a season ending injury. The Jets let his contract expire in 2026 and Cisco explored free agency before the Jets brought him back on a one year, $2.2 million deal. He was expected to compete with Dane Belton for the safety spot opposite Minkah Fitzpatrick, but Belton is clearly the better player. Fitzpatrick missed time early in the season, opening up playing time for Cisco, but Cisco did little with the opportunity. Once Fitzpatrick returned to action Cisco was relegated primarily to special teams play.

Over parts of two seasons Andre Cisco played 17 games for the Jets, starting 12. He racked up a total of 64 tackles, one sack, two passes defended, one sack, one forced fumble, three tackles for loss and one fumble recovery with the Jets. Cisco allowed an abysmal 115 passer rating in coverage during his time with the Jets.

The trade of Cisco opens up playing time for 2025 fourth round draft pick Malachi Moore in the short run. 2026 seventh round pick V.J. Payne also stands to benefit from the trade as he works his way back from a preseason injury that has kept him out of action so far this season.

item.title: Chargers Week 9 PFF Grades: Backups come out better than starters in lopsided loss
item.description: Derius Davis caught a touchdown pass and ended up the highest-graded player for the Chargers by Pro Football Focus.
item.content:encoded:
Even though the Chargers scored 22 points against the Texans, it somehow seemed like one of their worst outings of the year. Well, it sort’ve was before Quentin Johnston broke a short slant for a big 58-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter and the backups somehow found the end zone on their first drive of the game once they replaced the starting group.

Defensively, this was not a good game for Chris O’Leary’s unit but how can you blame a group looking a bit deflated after balling out for seven weeks just to see their offense make zero improvements two months into the year. I don’t blame them for flopping finally. It was bound to happen. The Texans receivers were also making crazy play after crazy play. Sometimes that happens!

But alas, 0-8 is still 0-8.

Let’s go ahead and check out the grades from Sunday.

Offense

Best

WR Derius Davis – 90.1
TE Charlie Kolar – 67.0
QB D.J. Uiagalelei – 65.2
OT Joe Alt – 63.8
RB Keaton Mitchell – 63.5

Davis posted his first elite game grade of his career on offense. He caught the second touchdown of the game from D.J. Uiagalelei, which was also the latter’s first career touchdown scored in the NFL. After the starting offense, including Justin Herbert, went 37 drives between touchdown drives, it took DJU and the backups just one! That’s pretty ugly!

Alt continues to be the team’s best offensive lineman. He allowed no sacks and two pressures.

Mitchell was an efficient player in his stats with some good chunk runs and a trio of passes caught which tied for the team lead on Sunday with Kolar.

Worst

FB Scott Matlock – 31.1
QB Justin Herbert – 46.3
RB Kimani Vidal – 48.0
C Jake Slaughter – 49.9
OT/G Alex Harkey – 51.6

Herbert threw his 11th interception of the season which also made it eight consecutive games with a pick thrown to begin this season. He did throw his sixth touchdown of the year, but even that was quite the lucky break when Johnston breaks one tackle on a five-yard slant and takes it 58 yards to the house.

Slaughter looked rough in this one in all phases. Specifically, there was a screen play to wideout Tre’ Harris who caught the pass in stride to then run behind Slaughter and Cole Strange out in front of him. Both linemen missed the first defender in pursuit and Harris was tackled before he could even get started.

Harkey was dealt a bad hand as he was forced to play right guard in place of the benched Strange who was initially replaced by Branson Taylor. Taylor was rolled up on after just nine plays and Harkey had to transition inside after spending most of this year at right tackle.

Defense

Best

LB Marlowe Wax – 91.3
DT Jamaree Caldwell – 79.3
EDGE Akkheem Mesidor – 77.7
DT Justin Eboigbe – 77.7
LB Daiyan Henley – 69.7

Wax made one of the best plays of the game for the defense when he made a diving pass deflection that ended up in the arms of Daiyan Henley.

Caldwell recorded the team’s best pass rush grade at 77.5. Mesidor had a top five grade in both run defense and pass rush.

With the aforementioned pick, Henley had one of his best games this year with every single one of his individual grades finishing at 60.0 or above.

Worst

CD Donte Jackson – 28.6
S Genesis Smith – 33.9
CB Tarheeb Still – 34.9
CB Rodney Shelley – 37.4
LB Troy Dye – 40.6

Jackson returned to the lineup for the first time since Week Four and he wound up being the worst-graded player on the Chargers against the Texans. His 29.0 coverage grade was his worst mark this year as he allowed four-of-six targets his way to be completed for 58 yards. He was also called for the penalty.

Smith posted a 19.0 tackling grade, by far his worst of the season. He had five previous tackling game grades above 75.0.

Still also posted his worst game of the season vs. the Texans. His 29.5 was by far his worst this year as he allowed seven completions on eight targets for 79 yards (also a season high) and a touchdown.

The cornerback room continued to look like chopped liver with Shelley also among the bottom five. That’s three cornerbacks in the red in a single week. However, Shelley did post great marks in tackling (79.3) and run defense (72.8).

item.title: Raiders make plays but cough up ball too much in 38-17 thumping to 49ers
item.description: When Las Vegas got within striking distance, turnovers scuttle hopes showcasing how far Silver & Black have to go
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders just couldn’t get out of their own way Sunday afternoon. Five awful second-half turnovers in a disconcerting 38-17 defeat were a testament to that.

Facing a well-oiled machine that the San Francisco 49ers are, the Silver & Black fell quickly behind 21-10 after generating just 48 yards through the air and 27 yards on the ground while yielding 123 passing and 125 rushing yards on defense.

And on its first offensive play of the second half, Las Vegas gifted San Francisco seven more points off quarterback Kirk Cousin’s pick six and just like that, 28-10 Niners, and turnover No. 1. The Raiders didn’t go away, however, and put together a solid nine-play, 69-yard scoring drive that culminated in tight end Brock Bowers climbing the ladder for a 21-yard touchdown dart from Cousins to trim the deficit to 28-17.

The Silver & Black gained even more momentum with rookie safety Treydan Stukes’ leaping interception of Brock Purdy. But just two plays later, linebacker Fred Warner punched the ball out of Bowers’ hands and the Red & Gold recovered, for Raiders turnover No. 2.

Again, Las Vegas refused to lay down and Rob Leonard’s much-maligned Raiders defense rose to the occasion stuffing Purdy on a QB sneak to get the ball back to Klint Kubiak’s offense. And it appeared the visitors from the desert were poised to get within four points of their former Bay Area rival when tight end Michael Mayer hauled in a sharp 24-yard pass from Cousins. But as the big pass catcher dove towards the goal line, he lost control of the ball fumbling it into the end zone with Warner recovering for the touchback. No points, and pivotal turnover No. 3.

Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers offense responded with a seven-play, 80-yard touchdown drive capped by Purdy’s 37-yard laser of a throw to Jordan Watkins for a pretty 37-yard touchdown catch in which the 49ers wide receiver boxed out rookie cornerback Hezekiah Masses.

Trailing 35-17, Kubiak’s offense once again got within striking distance on Raheem Morris’ stingy 49ers defense after Bowers’ 33-yard catch and run to the one-yard line. But the Nines read the QB sneak to perfection to stonewall that, an iffy offensive pass interference by Mayer cost the Raiders six points, and Cousins’ throw to Tre Tucker in the end zone was intercepted on 2nd-and-goal from the 13-yard line to thwart Kubiak’s offense once more — turnover No. 4.

After allowing a 49ers field goal, the Raiders ended the day offensively with another Cousins interception — a deep throw intended for Tucker that was picked off, turnover No. 5.

Las Vegas made it fair share of plays, but San Francisco simply made more and the defeat showcases just how far the Raiders are from competing with and beating good teams in the NFL. At 4-5 overall, Kubiak has done well to win four games in his rookie year as a head coach but those victories came against struggling teams. When faced with upper-echelon opposition, the Raiders have come close and no cigar or been boat raced.

Sunday afternoon in Santa Clara was a mix of both. Kubiak’s Raiders were in a dogfight and allowing just 10 second-half points against the 49ers is a plus. It’s just too bad Leonard’s defense couldn’t have that kind of performance in the opening half.

As I noted when I previewed the Raiders-49ers Week 9 matchup, the team that Kubiak wants in Las Vegas what Shanahan currently has in Santa Clara. The foundational model of a complementary football team that’s disciplined, efficient, and explosive in all three phases (offense, defense, and special teams) is what Kubiak eventually wants in the desert.

And today’s loss highlights fleeting moments of that but also the hideous warts of the complete opposite.

Let’s hit the quick slants as fast as both teams turned the ball to one another in a topsy turvy third quarter:

—The Niners’ 31 points on offense marks the sixth-straight time the Raiders defense has allowed 30 or more points this season — tying a modern era NFL record. Heading into Week 9 play, Las Vegas allowed 230 points total and only the Arizona Cardinals (238) and Baltimore Ravens (236) allowed more.

—A week after jumping too early in pass coverage (and not snagging two potential interceptions), Stukes displayed perfect timing and baiting Purdy on his interception of a pass intended for 49ers tight end George Kittle. The second-round pick is progressing well in his rookie year.

—Cousins finished 22 of 32 passing for 216 yards with one touchdown and three interceptions. Sunday’s performance was the worst the veteran quarterback put forth this season and it was a game where the 38-year-old’s arm strength waned as the game progressed.

—Even facing top-flight defenses, Bowers continues to be a productive Raider and un-guardable at times. The tight end hauled in seven passes for 111 yards and a touchdown (long of 33) to pace Las Vegas’ offense. Tucker finished behind Bowers with four receptions for 54 yards and Mayer had three catches for 37 yards.

—Las Vegas’ run game continues its abysmal performances finishing with 27 yards on 15 carries — three yards less than the first half sum of 27. Ashton Jeanty paced the group with six carries for 25 yards (long of nine) while Bowers added one carry for two yards, Cousins had two carries or no yards (but a touchdown) and Mike Washington Jr. finished with six totes for negative three yards.

—Raiders kick return man Dylan Laube continues to be a electric special teamer with seven returns for 197 yards (28.1 average per return) with a long of 57 yards. The Raiders first kick return was hauled in by Laube but he pitched it to wide receiver Dareke Young on a reverse for an additional 25 yards.

Quote of Note

“We’ll look at the film, and we’ll make our decisions when we have cool heads.”

—Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak on whether changes are needed to be made on defense after allowing 30 points for the sixth-straight week

“At this time of year, we’re focused on winning games. I really like our team. I don’t like losing games like this. You’ve got to have a lot more resilience to you when you’re playing a really good team that we played today. And when you start that slow, you don’t put yourself in good position. But I’m proud to coach the guys that we’re coaching.”

—Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak on the current state of his Raiders roster

Up Next

The 4-5 Raiders return to the confines of Allegiant Stadium in Week 10 to take on the visiting Seattle Seahawks. The home cooking hasn’t been too good for the Silver & Black as the team is just 1-3 inside Allegiant. Coming off a 17-3 win over the Arizona Cardinals in Week 9, the 5-4 Seahawks bring a team that Kubiak is all too familiar with. How that familiarity benefits his Raiders remains to be seen, however. A better showing and a win would lift Las Vegas back to .500 with a Week 11 AFC West showdown with the Denver Broncos on the horizon.

item.title: 49ers and Cowboys projected to be the highest-scoring game of the season
item.description: The 49ers are 4.5-point favorites over the Cowboys
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are third in the NFL in points per game. The Dallas Cowboys are sixth in the NFL. So it shouldn’t surprise you when oddsmakers like FanDuel Sportsbook make the total for these two teams the highest projected total of any game this season.

The projected total is set at 55.5. That ties for the highest total this season, with an October 12 matchup between the Bills and the Rams—a contest that ended 37-34. The Cowboys have had a couple of 54.5-point games. One was this month when they traveled to Arizona. That score was 30-33. The other 54.5 total came back in September against the Ravens, when the score was 34-31.

The 49ers have had only one pre-flop game projected north of 50. However, they’ve been involved in a couple of games that went over 60 points. When the total is as high as 55.5, the oddsmakers are telling us no number is high enough.

Low totals go under. High totals go over. “When it’s high, we go higher” is a saying in this market. That applies to two top-10 offenses.

The 49ers are 4.5-point favorites. That’s because only the Raiders are worse defensively in EPA per play than the Cowboys. Dallas ranks 25th in defensive success rate.

If you caught the Colts-Cowboys game on Sunday, the replays kept showing Daniel Jones throwing the ball underneath when receivers ran wide open at the intermediate and deep levels. Dallas was without cornerback Joey Porter Jr. and linebacker DeMarvion Overshown in Week 9. I’m not sure either will make much of a difference against the 49ers.

The 49ers have done a great job at limiting the damage this season defensively. But they have not played an offense with the weapons Dallas has to date. The secondary will be tested in ways they haven’t been all season, because it’ll be the best quarterback Raheem Morris has seen. Per Sports Info Solutions, no quarterback has been more valuable than Dak Prescott this season.

For as obnoxious as the total seems, it might be too low when you’re talking about these two high-powered offenses.

This game should be on Sunday Night Football. It has all of the makings of being the most entertaining game of the month. Too bad it wasn’t flexed.

item.title: NFL Injury Report, Week 10: Latest news, updates for Puka Nacua, Patrick Mahomes, more players for fantasy football
item.description: We go over the Week 10 NFL Injury Report, providing the latest updates and news, plus fantasy football analysis.
item.content:encoded:
It's the halfway point of the 2026 NFL season and by now you likely have weathered plenty of injuries on your fantasy football rosters. We have a handful of big names we're tracking going into Week 10 while four teams are on bye — the Bears, Broncos, Buccaneers and Eagles. Below we'll update you on the latest injury news, plus provide some useful fantasy football analysis.

Quarterback

  • Patrick Mahomes, KC (elbow)

  • J.J. McCarthy, NYG (hip)

  • Kyler Murray, MIN (hamstring)

  • Sam Darnold, SEA (quad/ribs) — Out for Week 10

  • Drew Lock, SEA (oblique) — Should be good to start

  • Justin Herbert, LAC (finger)

  • Deshaun Watson, CLE (concussion)

  • Malik Willis, MIA (groin)

Mahomes: At the time of Mahomes' injury in Week 9, it looked as though we were watching a QB who may be done for the season. But after exiting due to an elbow injury, Mahomes was able to return in the Chiefs' 35-12 win over the Jets on Sunday. Mahomes completed 23-of-31 passes for 242 yards and two scores, posting fewer than 20 fantasy points for the fifth time in the past six games.

Kenneth Walker III continues to be the focal point of the offense as the passing game lacks depth and a vertical threat. The Chiefs face the Falcons in Week 10 and Mahomes is considered "day to day" at this point. Should he sit, Justin Fields would draw the start, a downgrade for receivers like Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce. Walker would be relied on more heavily but could suffer with defenses keying in on the run game.

Seahawks QBs: Head coach Mike Macdonald already went on the radio Monday and said Darnold will be out Week 10 against the Raiders. Lock underwent tests on an oblique injury he suffered Sunday and those came back "good," so he's in line to start again. The Raiders have been a great fantasy matchup for QBs this season, allowing the fifth-most points to the position. However, the Seattle offense has struggled a bit with lack of depth behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Lock is back in the QB2 streaming convo for Sunday and isn't a bad spot start if you have Caleb Williams or Bo Nix on bye.

McCarthy: New York was able to sneak out of Philly on Sunday with a win. But McCarthy was forced to exit for a period of time to a hip injury. Head coach John Harbaugh has already told reporters McCarthy looks "like he's going to play" in Week 10 against Washington on TNF. The quick turnaround isn't ideal and we could see Jameis Winston back as the starter if McCarthy can't play.

The offense didn't look great against the Eagles, though they weren't much of a threat as the Giants' defense put the clamps on Joe Milton. We've seen both McCarthy and Winston elevate the passing game, so there isn't much change there in terms of how we approach Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely. Cam Skattebo should also be back to help the run game in Week 10 after missing Sunday's game. You were likely only starting McCarthy in deep superflex formats anyway.

Running Back

  • Rhamondre Stevenson, NE (knee)

  • TreVeyon Henderson, NE (illness)

  • Cam Skattebo, NYG (hamstring) — In line to return

  • Josh Jacobs, GB (finger)

Patriots RBs: Stevenson exited Sunday's blowout loss to the Packers early and did not return. Henderson has missed the past two games after being hospitalized due to "unexplained neurological symptoms." Stevenson is set to undergo an MRI on Monday and we'll see what the deal is. If Stevenson and Henderson are sidelined in Week 10 against the Lions in Germany, Corey Kiner would take over as the lead back. He finished with a solid 8-55-1 rushing line against Green Bay, though most of that production was on a fourth-quarter drive when the game was essentially over. Lan Larison would be the RB2 for New England, but the Pats could explore adding a back.

Jacobs: On the other side of that game, Jacobs suffered a fractured finger in the win over the Patriots and didn't return. Rushing duties were then split between Pierre Strong Jr. and Kaleb Johnson with MarShawn Lloyd out. Johnson rushed for 68 yards on 14 carries with a score. He looked pretty good running the ball for a team that has struggled to do so all season. But it was also in a blowout. Even so, Johnson is a proactive add off the waiver wire with Jacobs' status unclear. Head coach Matt LaFleur suggested there may be a way Jacobs plays through the fracture. Green Bay faces the Vikings in Week 10 before the bye, so the team could hold Jacobs out. If that's the case, it's hard to trust any Packers RB against one of the best defenses in the NFL.

Wide Receiver

  • Puka Nacua, LAR (knee)

  • Luther Burden III, CHI (concussion) — on bye

  • Ladd McConkey, LAC (back)

  • Jaylen Waddle, DEN (concussion) — on bye

  • Xavier Worthy, KC (hamstring)

  • George Pickens, DAL (hamstring)

  • Mike Evans, SF (Achilles)

  • DeVonta Smith, PHI (hamstring)

  • A.J. Brown, NE (knee)

  • Carnell Tate, TEN (shoulder)

  • Deebo Samuel Sr., SF (hamstring)

  • Garrett Wilson, NYJ (concussion)

Nacua: The Rams sent Nacua for an MRI and we'll see what those results reveal. It's not believed that the top wideout suffered a season-ending knee injury at this point. But Nacua could end up missing games. The Rams are already without Davante Adams and there isn't much depth behind those two. Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell and the trio of tight ends — Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen — would need to step up. LA could also lean more on its run game with Kyren Williams and Blake Corum.

If Nacua is out, it's a downgrade to the passing game and Matthew Stafford's fantasy outlook. It's a slight bump up for Williams and Corum, both of whom are involved in the passing game plenty. The Rams take on the Cardinals before their bye in Week 11, so chances are Nacua will at least be held out in Week 10. That'll give him ample time to rest the knee before Week 12 against the Packers.

Pickens: The Cowboys held Pickens out of their win over the Colts in Week 9. As a result, CeeDee Lamb went off for 10-195-1 while third-string WR Ryan Flournoy was quiet with two catches for 53 yards. Dallas leaned on the run game, leading most of the first half. It's clear the offense missed Pickens and will need him ready for a key NFC matchup with the Niners in Week 10. If Pickens is out again, Flournoy remains an a flex option while Lamb would remain a target hog and elite WR1.

item.title: Fantasy football buy, sell: 10 trade candidates for Week 10
item.description: Week 10 already? What a great opportunity to make some fantasy football trades.
item.content:encoded:
Week 10 of the fantasy football season always comes with some melancholy. Something about reaching that first double digit week really makes it seem like the season is almost done.

If you're feeling blue, spend 15 minutes today going through other rosters in your league. Find a rookie with upside on a bad team, or a veteran stuck on the bench of a good one. And with only a few more weeks left before the most common fantasy football trade deadlines (weeks 11-13), remember that the only thing that matters in the fantasy football regular season is making the playoffs. Whether you're a 1 or a 6 seed rarely matters if your team is hot at the right time.

So pick up the phone and make a deal. It's still only November, but a trade you make now could lead you to a championship.

Reminder that the Bears, Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers are on bye this week. Here are 10 fantasy football trade targets for Week 10:

Week 10 fantasy football players to buy

RB Tony Pollard, Titans

It would make so little sense for the 1-7 Titans to hold a 29-year-old RB who is a free agent in 2027. Even if Pollard isn't on the move, though, he's worth a buy coming out of Tennessee's bye. The Titans have a paper mache schedule to end the year, so you're either way, you're likely trading for a workhorse RB1 to end the year.

WR Zay Flowers, Ravens

Baltimore did not let rookie Joe Fagnano throw the ball on "Thursday Night Football" but did trade for Jacoby Brissett, who was routinely slinging it 35-50 times a game for the Cardinals. The veteran tends to lock in on his WR1s and helped Michael Wilson become a fantasy football league-winner in Arizona last year. Flowers has been putrid for two weeks but with Brissett, could have a similar finish in 2026.

RB Jonah Coleman, Broncos

We always love to buy rookies coming out of a bye, and Coleman might be obtainable this week with the Broncos off and rumors swirling about a potential trade for a veteran RB. Coleman hasn't cleared 60 rushing yards in a game yet and has been touchdown dependent, but if you can find a manager anxious about a veteran replacement, you should bet in the other direction.

RB Kyren Williams, Rams

Williams has been underwhelming enough the last month that his current manager might be looking to sell even though the Rams are just about out of receivers. Los Angeles being forced to commit to the ground while their pass catchers recover would only be a good thing for Williams.

TE Nate Boerkircher, Jaguars

The Jaguars' second round rookie TE is growing into a startable TE2. Boerkircher grabbed two catches for 61 yards in a win over the Ravens in Week 9 and was an inch away from catching a touchdown for the third straight game. He isn't earning many targets yet (three in Week 9 was a season high), but at 16 yards a catch and with wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. potentially on the move, Big Play Boerkircher could be the perfect guy to have on your bench come playoff time.

QB Carson Beck, Cardinals

Arizona coach Mike LaFleur can say whatever he wants in press conferences, but Gardner Minshew is an extremely mediocre backup and is not starting for this team for long. Beck might not be very good either, but he's a rookie and if he's starting before Thanksgiving, he's worth buying for cheap while still on the bench.

More: 32 things we learned in NFL Week 9: QB crises testing teams as backups flounder

Week 10 fantasy football players to sell

WR Matthew Golden, Packers

This is Golden's third straight appearance on the sell list despite him making me look foolish in Week 9 by catching all 10 of his targets for 164 yards and a touchdown. The second-year wideout has been great and I couldn't fault you for holding, but I maintain the opinion that his underlying receiving metrics point toward a player who is going to fade in the cold.

RB Christian McCaffrey, 49ers

Rookie Kaelon Black has quietly led San Francisco in rushing yards for the last two weeks while McCaffrey plays through a hamstring injury (and the superstar saw just three targets in Week 9). San Francisco is also now 7-1 and cares about nothing but a Super Bowl. Is there any incentive for the 49ers to give McCaffrey his normal workload in the regular season? If you can get a haul in return, consider it while he's still scoring touchdowns every week.

WR Kayshon Boutte, Texans

The first-year Texan had a nice game against the Chargers (4 catches for 125 yards and two scores) – but it's the Chargers, and Houston's passing offense is crowded enough that it might feature a different breakout receiver every week. Boutte hadn't topped 40 receiving yards in a game this season before this one and is a good sell high.

QB C.J. Stroud, Texans

At risk of being a Houston hater, Stroud threw for 11 touchdowns combined in his first seven games of the season and then 5 in Week 9. Even if Houston's passing attack is much improved, he's not doing that every week. Sell high!
